articles.text: Selling, leasing city land is a bad idea Editor: Following up my communication of September 11, thank you for providing a link to the updated Housing Element FAQs (https://www.piedmontishome. org/faqs). I am pleased to read that the City now is aware of, and intends to comply with, its obligations under California Government Code Section 37380. However, I am disappointed that the City continues to state that it “could sell or lease its land for low cost to an affordable housing developer”. We soon will need to spend tens of millions of dollars to upgrade the civic center (City Hall, police/fire, etc.), which will require increased taxes, issuance of one or more bonds (at interest rates that already are uncomfortably high), or some combination of the foregoing. City land should be conveyed for any use (affordable housing or otherwise) at fair market value so the proceeds will benefit all Piedmonters, rather than at a sweetheart price that benefits the recipient of the land. On July 20, the Piedmont Post published a resident’s letter to the City Council that called for a legal battle against the Housing Element. A below-market-rate land conveyance would invite such a lawsuit. The City would spend tens or hundreds of thousands of dollars on legal fees, and the housing project would be delayed by months or years. In summary, selling or leasing City land at below market rate is a bad idea. Don’t do it. –Dana Shultz The following letter was set to the Piedmont Planning Department. Editor: As a candidate running for Piedmont school board, I stand with Ruchi Medhekar in condemning non-transparent and divisive political websites and communications. In last week’s Piedmont Post, Ruchi rightfully declared her opposition to those who hide behind anonymity and degrade civil discourse in our community, and I wholeheartedly agree with her. If elected, one of my main priorities for PUSD will be to increase transparency at all levels. It is critical that we create a culture of trust and accountability so that stakeholders are knowledgeable about district spending, processes, curriculum, and initiatives and are collectively invested in the outcomes. This means giving ample opportunities for stakeholder engagement and proactively gathering parents, teachers, administrators, and other community members around a table to listen, learn, and discuss with honesty and respect. One way to do this would be through PUSD school board sub-committees or commissions similar to Piedmont City Council’s Park Commission, Planning Commission, and the Bond Oversight Committee – all of which report to our city council. These groups are made up of community members who apply and are then selected by the City Council to serve for their subject matter expertise for a set term limit. Each of these bodies provides recommendations to the Council on policies and projects, and some make decisions on matters specifically delegated to them. articles.text: Editor: I met Jen shortly after her family moved to Piedmont. Over time, we became friends, exposing me to the very same qualities I suspect compelled City Council to award Jen the vacated seat she sought. Jen was most certainly selected because of her experience as an attorney with a law degree from Howard University. The Council was likely also impressed by her exemplary leadership qualities as a highly engaged member of the community, a founding member of the Piedmont Racial Equity Campaign (PREC) and co-president of the Piedmont Anti-Racism and Diversity Committee (PADC). Yet I’m sure Jen’s interpersonal qualities probably swayed the Council as well. Her easy manner, her adept approach to solving problems, the simplicity with which she lays down her vision, her receptivity to opinion, and a kindness that infuses her social discourse. I saw all of these qualities the day Jen interviewed to fill the vacant City Council seat nine months ago. I have also personally experienced these qualities as friends, working closely together when Jen served as co-president with PADC and when I worked with her on Veronica Anderson Thigpen’s School Board campaign where Jen served as campaign manager. I saw her inspire our team and execute on strategy. articles.text: eq8iQH3Nxiq4SUStmQ/viewform Piedmont’s Sustainability Division is seeking input from residents on a pilot home electrification rebate program, which is anticipated to launch in January 2023. The Piedmont City Council allocated $50,000 in the 2022- 23 City budget to develop a pilot rebate program that would provide incentives for residents to replace polluting gas appliances with clean electric alternatives. The intent of the pilot program is two-fold: to educate residents on available electric appliance options and to help them make the transition in a cost-effective manner. The intention is to offer local rebates beyond what is available through state and regional programs for the proper removal and replacement of natural gas appliances with high efficiency electric units. Eligible low-income residential applicants may qualify for additional funding. The survey is an attempt to gauge Piedmonters’ knowledge about and plans for home electrification, and asks for residents to share their thoughts on questions such as: • Are you planning to replace gas appliances like cooktops, furnaces, dryers, and water heaters with electric alternatives? • What types of information or assistance would most encourage you to electrify your home? • What are your biggest concerns about switching to electric appliances? • Do you support or oppose a local rebate program? How much of a rebate makes sense for each type of appliance? Please take a few minutes to fill out the survey. Responses are anonymous. Docs.google.com/ forms/d/e/1FAIpQLSfcmwRWnnUUCWzjpp2mgM82s-fSqJ2IOne of the largest contributors to Piedmont’s community greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions is natural gas use in residential buildings. Natural gas is mostly methane, a GHG that is approximately 84 times more potent than Carbon Dioxide (CO2). The use of natural gas for space heating and water heating in particular, significantly contribute to a household’s GHG emissions (~90%). In addition, leaks in the natural gas distribution infrastructure are common, thereby releasing methane directly into the atmosphere. In the last three years, emissions from natural gas use in Piedmont’s residential buildings exceeded 14,000 metric tons of CO2 equivalent per year. This is equivalent to roughly 14,000 round-trip flights of 3000-miles (from San Francisco to New York and back). In order to reduce natural gas emissions and meet Piedmont’s climate action goals, the community must switch to electric appliances. Electrification refers to the process of replacing everything that burns fossil fuels with efficient electric alternatives. By removing your natural gas appliances, you reduce GHG emissions and improve indoor air quality. Electric alternatives are available, affordable, and market-ready such as heat pumps and induction stoves. Learn more about the costs, benefits, and funding opportunities for electrifying your home on the City’s website. Piedmont.ca.gov/ services___departments/planning___building/about_building_/electrification. Alyssa Dykman is the City of Piedmont’s Sustainability Program Manager. “Our CEO is having a downer.”

Natural gas is mostly methane, a GHG that is approximately 84 times more potent than Carbon Dioxide (CO2). The use of natural gas for space heating and water heating in particular, significantly contribute to a household’s GHG emissions (~90%). In addition, leaks in the natural gas distribution infrastructure are common, thereby releasing methane directly into the atmosphere. In the last three years, emissions from natural gas use in Piedmont’s residential buildings exceeded 14,000 metric tons of CO2 equivalent per year. This is equivalent to roughly 14,000 round-trip flights of 3000-miles (from San Francisco to New York and back). In order to reduce natural gas emissions and meet Piedmont’s climate action goals, the community must switch to electric appliances. Electrification refers to the process of replacing everything that burns fossil fuels with efficient electric alternatives. By removing your natural gas appliances, you reduce GHG emissions and improve indoor air quality. Electric alternatives are available, affordable, and market-ready such as heat pumps and induction stoves. articles.text: The Piedmont League of Women Voters will host a discussion about the impact of textiles on the climate. Rebecca Burgess, Executive Director of Fibershed, will present an online talk entitled “Understanding the Climate Impact of Textiles” on Thursday, October 19, at 4:00 p.m. Ever wonder about the impact on the climate of the textiles in your closet – from production to manufacturing to retail distribution? Come learn how sustainable fashion and regenerative farming are closely linked, how new programs are making a difference, and what you can do to reduce the carbon footprint of the clothes you wear and the fabrics you use. Burgess has two decades of experience working with ecology, fiber systems, and regional economic development. She is the author of the best-selling books Harvesting Color: How to Find Plants and Make Natural Dyes, and Fibershed: Growing a Movement of Farmers, Fashion Activists, and Makers for a New Textile Economy. She has taught at Westminster College, Harvard University, and California College of the Arts. She is on the board of the Livestock Conservancy and is on the Textile expert Rebecca Burgess leadership council of the Center for Regenerative Agriculture and Resilient Systems at Chico State University. This event is part of the League’s 2022 Climate Speaker Series and is co-sponsored by Leagues in Oakland and Solano Counties. This talk will be held live on Zoom and YouTube and will include an audience Q&A session. For details and for access to the Zoom presentation, visit the website lwvpiedmont.org. The event is free and open to the public.

What else can the school district do now and what needs to be done moving forward to recruit and retain the highest quality teachers in Piedmont? neurship • cryptology • game theory I would also like to explore increasing our foreign language offerings at all grade levels, including in elementary school. 2 Retaining Teachers Research shows that an effective teacher is the most important factor contributing to student achievement. Ensuring we offer competitive teacher compensation packages – both pay and benefits – is critical. We should review PUSD’s budget annually to identify changes and compromises we must make to pay our teachers a competitive wage with PUSD’s limited resources while advocating for the state to provide sufficient funds for all districts to compensate educators adequately. When a teacher leaves the district, we should conduct an exit interview to understand why they are leaving. We should actively work to find solutions to prevent further attrition. We should be leaders, instead of following what other districts do. PUSD used to be a highly sought after district for teachers. Conducting win/ loss interviews with candidates would help us understand what motivates high quality teachers. We should improve the pay schedule especially for teachers earlier on in their careers with less tenure. Many of our teachers will be retiring soon, and we will struggle to replace them with newer teachers when the wages are less competitive than proximal districts. Your idea for a new course at PUSD? There is a vital need for today’s kids to ask critical questions of data and to recognize when data is being misused - in short to be data literate. Integrating data science into a robust subject matter will benefit all high school students, and there are tools to make these techniques accessible - for example, simplified coding packages (e.g. RStudio) and visualization tools. In Data Analysis in Climate Science, students would learn how the data available to climate scientists has evolved over time, and how computer modeling has facilitated its analysis. Students would develop a specific research question and use free primary data sources (e.g. federal and state government) to aid in the process. One example could be to determine changes in fire severity in Northern California. At the end of the term, students would present a final project using data that supported their findings SHIRLEY HOOI 1. Your idea for a new course at PUSD? Besides financial literacy, I believe these are fundamental needs every student should possess upon high school graduation. 2. Retaining Teachers To recruit and retain teachers, the district will need to continue to offer a competitive compensation package, a supportive workplace and a defined vertical career pathway of advancement within the district. In addition, I believe that the district should empower Piedmont teachers to make decisions on how best to teach their students based upon their own values, while taking into consideration the beliefs and values of students and stakeholders. articles.text: Almost Famous: Queen of Basketball is about Lucy Harris, arguably the greatest women’s basketball player. Title IX, the federal legislation enacted 50 years ago, is a 37-word snippet tucked into the Educational Amendments of 1972: “No person in the United States shall, on the basis of sex, be excluded from participation in, be denied the benefits of, or be subjected to discrimination under any education program or activity receiving Federal financial assistance.” It is no exaggeration to say that those 37 words led to a revolution in women’s education – from middle school shop class to graduate school admissions – but nowhere more visible than in women’s sports. The Piedmont Appreciating Diversity Film Series will return to in-person screenings this November with two award-winning short films that trace both the drama of the law’s passage, and the effect it had on athletes: Mink! and Almost Famous: Queen of Basketball. Both films were directed by Canadian filmmaker Ben Proudfoot, a multiple Oscar nominee for his documentary shorts. He won an Oscar in 2022 for Queen of Basketball. Mink! focuses on Patsy Takemoto Mink, the first woman of color elected to Congress, who faces racial and gender discrimination at every stage of her career. The film begins with Mink’s daughter’s words: “The future of equality in some large way was on the table that day when the personal and political collided,” setting up the drama that is the film’s centerpiece. Director Proudfoot recounts learning about the history of Title IX, and the formidable campaign to dilute or erode the law. The film portrays Mink’s compelling fight to save the crucial language, and how it almost lost for lack of a single vote – her own. Almost Famous: Queen of Basketball is a similarly inspiring short film about a remarkable athlete who came of age just after Title IX was passed. Lucy Harris was arguably the greatest women’s basketball player: she won three national trophies; she played in the ’76 Olympics; and she was drafted to the NBA. None of that would have happened without Title IX. But have you heard of her? Her story is told in her own endearing words. NBA players Steph Curry and Shaquille O’Neal served as executive producers. Both films will be shown in person on Thursday, November 3, at 7 p.m. at the Ellen Driscoll Playhouse at Havens School, 325 Mink! focuses on Patsy Takemoto Mink, the first woman of color elected to Congress. Highland Avenue. Following the films, Chelle Putzer and Eva Phalen of the Piedmont Recreation Department will discuss their efforts to bring equality to girls’ sports, and the effect of Title IX on women’s sports today. After the screenings, Chelle Putzer, Director of Piedmont Recreation Department, and Recreation Supervisor Eva Phalen will speak about what’s working to promote equal opportunities for girls in sports, and why it matters throughout life. As always, the screening and discussion are free. Masks will be required to help ensure the safety of the audience. Appreciating Diversity Film Series is an all-volunteer nonprofit organization that has presented free screenings to the community for 25 years. For more information, visit diversityfilmseries.org, or contact Deborah@diversityfilmseries.org

articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. The Post will publish the weekly street sweeping schedule from now through February, 2023. articles.text: Staff Photos Declan Linnane had two assists against Encinal. He talks about the team’s outlook while rolling 5-0 in WACC competition. Piedmont’s boys’ water polo team continued a strong start to its season with a 10-7 win over the Encinal Jets in Alameda on Thursday, September 29. The Highlanders remain undefeated in league at 5-0 and 10-2 overall. They still have to face league opponents Alameda and Bishop O’Dowd. “We’re trying to build up for league championships and North Coast Section. Our goal in the beginning of the season was to do well in both of those tournaments. I think we are in the driver’s seat,” said first-year head coach Rik Krumins. “We also need to continue maintaining the pace at practice and working out little tweaks here and there. We’re doing some new things on offense, working on the defense, and working on the fundamentals. When we get to the postseason, hopefully we’ll be ready to go,” Declan Linnane has been a huge part of the team’s success this season. “Right now, we’re just trying to get better each game. A lot of guys are getting reps right now and we’re going to need them down the road,” said Linnane. In Thursday’s game, Piedmont led 7-2 by the end of the first quarter with their starters in the pool and then gave younger players the remaining three quarters to gain experience. “We want to let our starters begin the game and then get our subs and bench players to get time and play the entire game. It’s a great experience; it’s building up those guys to give them match experience,” said Krumins. Game Recap Piedmont opened the game with Encinal with six goals and 7-2 lead after one period. Encinal cut the deficit 8-5 by halftime and continued to narrow the score at 9-7 at the start of the fourth quarter. Piedmont’s defense stepped up in the end to concede no goals and win 10-7. Within the first 1:15 of action George Stein scored a goal. Twenty seconds later Daniel Banin scored on an assist from Declan Linnane. Following a Finn Burke had three goals against Encinal. Evan Dickason had two goals against the Jets. save by goalkeeper Dariush Kashani, he threw a long pass to Linnane, who sent a pass into Finn Burke in the hole set for a close-range goal. With 4:29 left in the quarter, Burke scored on a five-meter penalty shot. A minute later, Banin scored, followed by Elles Krieckhaus getting on the scoreboard on an assist by Stein a minute and a half later. After allowing two goals by Encinal, Kashani made a save in the closing seconds of the first quarter and scored by sending a shot the length of the pool into an open net for a 7-1 lead. Evan Dickason opened the second quarter with a goal in 13 seconds on a five-meter penalty shot. It was the last time PHS would score in the half. Piedmont scored once in the third quarter with Leo Hurwitz assisting Burke with 3:54 left in the third. Starting the fourth quarter with a tenuous 9-7 lead, PHS peppered the Jets goal, forcing their goalie to make three saves in close quarters. Dickason scored by netting one with 1:32 on the clock. Final stats: Burke scored three goals. Banin and Dickason scored twice. Stein had a goal and an assist. Linnane had two assists. Krieckhaus scored once. Hurwitz had an assist. articles.text: Piedmont High’s girls’ tennis team continued its strong season last week with two victories at their home courts; a 5-2 win over NCS rival College Prep on Tuesday, September 27 and 4-3 over Western Alameda County Conference opponent Alameda on Wednesday, September 28. The win over College Prep will help boost Piedmont in the Division 2 NCS standings, while the victory over the Hornets comes against perhaps their best competition in the WACC. “We had two good victories this week defeating CPS and Alameda Wednesday. CPS is a D2 school, so this win will help our NCS position. Alameda may be our toughest league opponent, them and possibly Bishop O’Dowd, so this is good for us,” said coach Jim Landes. Against Alameda, the clinching fourth victory came from the No. 3 doubles team of freshmen Kate Jumper and Arianna Kortum with dominant scores of 6-1, 6-1. “We were in a good mindset and were really positive, I think that helped. I try not to focus too much on the score, but it feels good to know that we could do something good for the team as a whole,” said Jumper. “I think it went really well because we were both hitting well and went out there with the same goal of hitting volleys and being more aggressive. Winning was really encouraging, not just for us Staff Photos Tanya Kononova is on a winning streak at No. 1 singles. She defeated Alameda’s top player, Sonam Manghai, 6-1, 6-2 and College Prep’s No. 1 singles player 6-2, 6-2. but for the entire team. The fact that everyone has so much potential, it feels good to get this done,” added Kortum. No. 1 singles starter Tanya Kononova was victorious in both of her matches, defeating College Prep’s Juliana Johnson 6-2, 6-2 and Alameda 6-1, 6-2. articles.text: Beats El Cerrito 11-5, Moreau Catholic 8-7, falls to Marin Academy Photos by Nancy Brahm Piedmont’s girls’ water polo team won two of three games at the Battle of the Bay tournament at Encinal on the weekend of September 30 - October 1. The girls’ water polo team had a successful run at the Battle of the Bay tournament at Encinal High in Alameda last weekend, September 30-October 1. It won two of its three games, defeating El Cerrito 11-5 and Moreau Catholic 8-7 on Saturday, after losing 14-5 to Marin Academy on the opening day. The tournament proved to be a showcase for Katarina Melian and Rosie Feldman, each of whom scored 10 goals in two days of action. 11-5 win over El Cerrito Piedmont was first on the board after a minute and a half when Feldman assisted Annika Nilsson on a fast break. Following a Gaucho five-meter penalty shot with 3:14 left in the first, Odessa Dando took advantage of a 6-on-5 opportunity with 2:25 left for a 2-1 score. In the second quarter, Katarina Melian scored on a five-meter penalty. El Cerrito scored two minutes later to make it 3-2, but with a man-advantage, Melian made it 4-2 with just 34 seconds on the clock. Melian scored once again as time at halftime to take a 5-2 lead. It was all Rosie Feldman in the third quarter. The PHS sharpshooter scored four consecutive goals to boost Piedmont’s lead to 9-2 heading into the last period. El Cerrito scored 30 seconds into the fourth, and Melian scored on a five-meter penalty shot for a 10-3 lead. The Gauchos scored 30 seconds later, but Kate Meyjes responded with a goal at the 1:55 mark. El Cerrito scored the game’s final goal with 18 seconds left to play. 8-7 win over Moreau The Highlanders opened with a goal by Feldman within two minutes. Moreau equalized 30 seconds later, followed by Melian’s goal on a man-advantage. Feldman scored again at 3:23 mark to go up 3-1. Moreau made it 3-2 less than 20 seconds later but Feldman kept PHS on top at 4-2 with 1:56 to play in the quarter. Both teams were scoreless in the second quarter with strong defense by both sides. In the third quarter Moreau battled back to tie the match at 4-4 with 5:10 left in the period, but Feldman scored on a lob shot at 4:14 mark to regain the lead. Melian extended the advantage to 6-4 on another 6-on-5 opportunity with two minutes left. At the 1:23 mark, Moreau scored a five-meter penalty to cut it to 6-5. One minute later Melian responded to take a 7-5 lead. In an exciting, tension-filled fourth quarter, Moreau came to life with 4:31 left in the game, scoring two consecutive goals to tie the match at 7-7. But 20 seconds later, Melian scored what proved to be the winning goal, 8-7. In the remaining four minutes, goalie Friedie Schickedanz made a number of big stops, including saving a final shot at the buzzer. Katarina Melian scored 10 goals in three games.

articles.text: Photo by Rob Peterson The girls’ volleyball team defeated San Leandro 3-1 on Homecoming Night. It was standing room only at Binks Rawlings Gym on Friday night, September 30. The occasion was the girls’ volleyball team playing a match with San Leandro, and more importantly taking the place of the football team for Homecoming night. With the cancelation of the football team’s game on Friday, the volleyball team happily rescheduled a match with the Pirates to Piedmont and delighted the packed house with a 3-1 victory. The win was made even more special with PHS pep band, cheerleaders, and decorations throughout the gym. “We fed off of our amazing crowd; we had the band there, cheerleaders there, and a packed student section,” said coach Mariah Cardenas. “The girls came in super strong. We started with our strongest rotation, Bauer [Peterson] as setter, Shelby [Cavenaugh] right side, Bree [DeYoung] middle, Sadie [Town] as DS, and Klara [Zietlow] as libero. Eden [Lorin] has been playing libero, but the past couple of games it’s been pretty evident that Eden is a killer on the outside. I’m definitely utilizing Eden playing front and back row. Klara is the only sophomore on the team, and she has taken over the role of libero.” In the first set, Piedmont trailed 2-0 but turned the tide to score six straight points to jump ahead 6-2 and then scored eight of the next 11 points gain a commanding 14-5 lead with help from an ace by Sadie Town and kills by Tara Kothari, Eden Lorin, and Shelby Cavenaugh. From there, Piedmont went ahead 19-9 and then at 20-12, scored five of the next six points to win 25-13 with the help of strong serving by Lorin and a finishing kill by Town. Piedmont lost the 2nd set 27-25. The two sides traded points in the early going but Piedmont eventually pulled away to hold a six-point 15-9 lead. The Pirates inched away at the lead at 19-15, where Town gained two more kills during that span. Following a kill by Kothari, PHS held set-point at 24-21 but conceded four straight points to trail 25-24. articles.text: Piedmont’s football team reached the North Coast Section Semifinals in 2014, won the won a WACC Shoreline title, and finished with a 12-1 record. It’s been a tumultuous time for Piedmont High’s football program for several years. Wrought with low roster turnout, the team has faced problems of being able to field a complete varsity team for three years. Since the departure of former coach James Holan after the 2017 season, there’s been a sharp downturn for the Highlanders. Long gone are the days of consistent North Coast Section appearances. Covid and the pandemic pretty well knocked the football team off its mooring for at least two years, with a residual effect in this, the third year of a struggle for survival. Holan left Piedmont High with an overall record of 24-13 from 2015-2017, and was 18-7 as a coordinator in 2013 and 2014 under Scott Coats. Piedmont has qualified for the post-season North Coast Section playoffs every year from 2011 until 2018 under John Trotman. Between 2013-2017 Piedmont never finished with a losing record. In 2014 under Coats, its most successful coach in a5 years, PHS went 12-1 overall, reached the Division 4 NCS Semifinals, and won the WACC Shoreline championship. The following year Piedmont went 9-3 overall, reached the quarterfinals of the NCS playoffs, and won a second consecutive WACC Shoreline championship. The team then was bumped up to the WACC Foothill Division, where they resided until the spring of 2021 when the Mission Division was created during a topsy-turvy Covid-impacted sports year. 2014 marked the first time in 38 years Piedmont won a league title. Gabe Watson, the school’s All-Time leading rusher, went on to play for the University of Sioux Falls and was a candidate for the Harlon Hill Trophy, considered the Heisman Trophy for Div. 2 schools. In 2016, Piedmont posted a 8-5 record and advanced to the Div. 4 Former Piedmont football coach Jerome Johnson. Staff Photo Staff Photo Piedmont last reached the NCS postseason in 2019 under coach John Trotman, now the head coach at St. Mary’s in Berkeley. NCS semifinals before falling to No. 1 seed Cardinal Newman. In Holan’s last year at the school in 2017, PHS went 7-5 and reached the quarterfinals of the NCS playoffs before losing to No. 3 Harker in San Jose. In 2019 under Trotman, Piedmont had a 5-6 record and qualified for the NCS playoffs as a No. 7 seed. They were upset by No. 10 Justin-Siena in the first round. Trotman resigned, which opened the door for former defensive coordinator Jerome Johnson to be promoted to head coach from defensive coordinator. PHS went 3-7 the following season with a roster of largely JV players. But in the spring of 2021, the hybrid Covid-impacted high school sports season when football was played in the spring, the Highlander varsity was undefeated at 5-0 under Johnson. It was the first winning season since 2017. However, the impact of Covid resulted in a low turnout of players, leading to the high school canceling the junior varsity program. In the fall of 2021, the team finished with a 2-7 overall record with only 17 players. PHS Athletic Director Bradley Smet informed other teams in the Western Alameda County Conference that Piedmont would be canceling its varsity program and let coach Johnson go. The decision, when parents heard about it, led to an effort to revive football. Now at 0-5 for the current season, the varsity program is on the verge of a full cancelation. The Homecoming game was canceled due to mounting injuries and a depleted roster of a team that began the season with 20 players. Football began at Piedmont High in 1921, and for the first time in 100 years it played the season without a league, scheduling games as an independent school. And now, Piedmont High must again look for answers to revive interest in the sport.

articles.text: Paula Vogel’s new play is based on the real-life events of Sholem Asch’s Broadway debut of The God of Vengeance. Although many consider Asch’s work to be a seminal work of Jewish culture, it is also viewed by some as traitorous libel. “We were lucky enough to be on hand when Paula Vogel’s Indecent opened on Broadway five years ago, and being huge fans of hers already, and galvanized by the production, we began angling to present the play’s Bay Area premiere immediately,” said San Francisco Playhouse Artistic Director Bill English. “At the time we were a long shot due to strong interest from bigger companies, but after a two-year pandemic and catastrophic changes in the American theatre, a door opened five years later for us to present Indecent.” The play is directed by Susi Damilano, with music direction by Dmitri Gaskin and choreography by Nicole Helfer. The principal cast members include Dean Linnard, Billy Cohen, Rachel Botchan, and Rivka Borek. Indecent is co-produced with the Yiddish Theatre Ensemble and features a live klezmer score. “It is both a love song to the Ashkenazi Jewish culture spanning 50 years, and a love song to the theatre. It is an odyssey that spins us from Warsaw to Berlin, to NY Yiddish theatre, to Broadway and back to Warsaw as the tumultuous and tragic history of the early 20th Century unfolds around the play within our play,” English said. articles.text: SF Symphony masters Mahler Review by Paul Hertelendy Mahler’s “Resurrection” was a revelation, leaving us in the audience limp and giddy, as if, in a euphoric state of ecstasy, we had just been led through the Pearly Gates into the great beyond. It was the finest hour yet for Maestro Esa-Pekka Salonen in the bows when the orchestra remained steadfastly seated, deflecting the cheers to the conductor himself. The audience too responded with an inordinate five-minute ovation for the San Francisco Symphony and Chorus for their rousing concert. In a budget-be-damned September 27 concert, it ran 24 minutes beyond the two-hour norm, most likely unleashing overtime rewards for all concerned in the oversize ensemble. Mahler’s Symphony No. 2 does require oversize forces – two harps, five percussionists, close to a score of brass players, with various brass sounding from offstage sites above and outside the Davies Hall auditorium, adding to a sense of some reimagined fourth-dimension wonderworld. The disappointment was that all this magnificence overshadowed a significant world premiere by Trevor Weston, Push, that had gone before. The genius of Gustav Mahler lay not so much in the Resurrection choral-vocal text that he himself had penned in the late 19th century. It was in the entire 90-minute structure of a dozen moods culminating in that euphoric finale rivaling in impact Beethoven’s parallel Ninth Symphony (cum chorus) of some 75 years earlier. In the build-up, Mahler leads us through a welter of emotions of a very real life and world, overemotional yet precise in his scores: a serene sunrise on violins, then on to the charming Austrian forerunner of the waltz called Lȁndler, on to fullthroated, exuberant outpourings on brass and percussion at deafening levels. It was an excitement akin to jumping off a high diving board willy-nilly without checking if the pool contained water. On the podium, Salonen paid inordinate attention to dynamics – not only loud, but also with some of the softest and most intimate sonics heard at Davies Hall. This was a throwback to unadulterated romanticism with visceral effect as rarely heard in our very rational 21st century. There came too the Mahler-tradeSan Francisco Symphony music director Esa-Pekka Salonen. marked stimulus of pulse-quickening up-bows on violins, the bells-high positioning of French horns, and amazing crescendos. This was a quasi-religious experience comparable to high mass at a reverberent Gothic cathedral in Mahler’s own Bohemia-Austria habitats. Much of the impact came from the 110 voices of the Symphony Chorus sounding out as rarely before under Salonen and guest chorus leader Jenny Wong. Just the male contingent alone had emerged with such robust strength that the walls of Davies may still be reverberating. In far more restrained solos came soloists Michelle DeYoung and a newcomer from South Africa, Golda Schultz. One lamented that none of the night’s singing of consonants was well enough enunciated to enable following the German text in the printed program. Trevor Weston’s Push Almost lost in the night’s embers was the world premiere that went before, Trevor Weston’s Push, which deserved a better spotlight. Push refers to a Dvorak quote about Americans’ pushing the envelope in their endeavors. Though teaching on the East Coast, the 55-year-old Black composer Weston has a considerable East Bay history, having earned his Ph.D. with the eminent late Prof. Olly Wilson at UC Berkeley, and having then associated with the Oakland Symphony’s late maestro, Michael Morgan, whose versatile involvement in so many facets of community music demands updating all the monographs on a conductor’s role. His deft threnody in the four-movement piece was dedicated to Morgan, who died last year at 63 shortly before his scheduled SF Symphony debut. (At times it was definitely tougher to make it as a Black musician, whether Morgan, Wilson or Weston. In 1975 I heard the 17-year-old ill-attired Morgan in a young conductors’ competition for the Baltimore Symphony leading a Brahms movement and competing against all-white competition typically five years older and with diplomas from leading institutions. I heard Morgan give an electric reading, evoking play surpassing anything from the other candidates. However, he only got an honorable mention, with a music prof afterward citing to me Morgan’s crude stick technique!) Weston demonstrated an apt versatility, ranging from popjazz influences to subtle orchestral expressiveness. The latter was also evident in his subdued “City Quiet” segment hovering somewhere between Copland and Bartok in pianissimos. The outer movements were boisterous, punctuated by effusiveness akin to John Coltrane, whom Weston could only hear on recordings, as tenor saxist Coltrane had perished at age 40 the year Weston was born. MUSIC NOTES The SFS’ new principal cellist, Rainer Eudeikis, performed in the first chair. Among the remaining unfilled principal chairs are flute and harp, with substitutes filling in each time. A Piedmont resident, Paul Hertelendy also writes on classical concerts at the arts-review web site www.artsSF.com Trevor Weston’s 20-minute world premiere, Push; Mahler’s Symphony No. 2 with the S.F. Symphony and Chorus. Esa-Pekka Salonen, music director, at Davies Hall, San Francisco, September 29 through October 2. For SFS info, call (415) 864-6000, or go online: www.sfsymphony.org.

articles.text: $35 million donation initiates renaming The American Conservatory Theater (ACT) in San Francisco has been renamed the Toni Rembe Theater after the longtime San Francisco fine arts philanthropist. The renaming is in recognition of an anonymous donor who gifted the theater $35 million, the largest single gift in ACT’s history. The announcement was made on September 20 by the theater’s Executive Director. Jennifer Bielstein, Artistic Director Pam MacKinnon, Board Chair Jeff Minick, and Board President Joaquín Torres. “We are deeply grateful to the generous donor for this extraordinary gift,” said Bielstein. “The funds provided are transformational for the future of American Conservatory Theater and the impact of our programming throughout the San Francisco Bay Area. Toni is a role model, and we are honored to recognize her in such a deserving and significant way. The Toni Rembe Theater will forever serve as a reminder of Toni’s decades-long contributions to the arts community.” Toni Rembe is a longtime philanthropist in the arts and has maintained positions as president of the van Lӧben Sels/Rembe Rock Foundation, a private foundation specializing in the promotion of social justice through legal services; a co-founder and advisory board member of the Rock Center for Corporate Governance at Stanford University; a founding member of the Theatre Communication Group’s National Council for the American Theater; and a member of the board of the Immigrant Legal Resource Center. She currently serves on the board of trustees for ACT for over two decades. “Toni Rembe has been central to the health and well-being of the Bay Area theater scene,” said MacKinnon. “Her wide-ranging artistic taste and appreciation of artists and the special act of audiences coming together for a story make her a true theater lover. Her generosity and commitment to Bay Area culture and artmaking is unparalleled.” Photo courtesy of KQED The ACT Theater has been renamed after fine arts philanthropist Toni Rembe.
articles.title: ACT Theater renamed Toni Rembe Theater

articles.text: Filoli House and Gardens in Woodside is celebrating “Orchard Days” every weekend through October 30. Visit the gardens this fall and stroll through the seven-acre Gentleman’s Orchard, a vital component of self-sustaining estates and a feature of many American country houses at the turn of the century. The acres hold a collection of fruits grown for leisure rather than commercial production. The Bourns, the original owners of the estate, planted their orchard with 1,000 trees – apples, pears, plums, apricots, walnuts, figs, and quinces. Only 115 trees remained when the orchard was restored, but there are now over 500 fruit and nut trees of various species. Filoli staff preserve the historic collection of rare and historically significant varieties. Orchard Days at Filoli feature live music, and food and drink for purchase at the Bluebird Bar. Reservations are required. To purchase tickets, visit https:// filoli.org/orchard-days/. The gardens are open daily from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. Filoli House and Garden hosts Orchard Days every weekend through October 30.

Weekend Orchard Days at Filoli through October 30 By Allyson Aleksey Filoli House and Gardens in Woodside is celebrating “Orchard Days” every weekend through October 30. Visit the gardens this fall and stroll through the seven-acre Gentleman’s Orchard, a vital component of self-sustaining estates and a feature of many American country houses at the turn of the century. The acres hold a collection of fruits grown for leisure rather than commercial production. The Bourns, the original owners of the estate, planted their orchard with 1,000 trees – apples, pears, plums, apricots, walnuts, figs, and quinces. Only 115 trees remained when the orchard was restored, but there are now over 500 fruit and nut trees of various species. Filoli staff preserve the historic collection of rare and historically significant varieties. Orchard Days at Filoli feature live music, and food and drink for purchase at the Bluebird Bar. articles.text: Opera has always been the most popular form of classical music. It combines every aspect of music drama and art. There is good reason why people love opera. When opera addresses human tragedy, people understand it’s a theater of the absurd. When opera addresses comedy, it’s the other way around. Thus, success is guaranteed. Adding insult to injury, opera singers always made much more money than other musicians. They were the pop stars of days gone by. We have many fine opera companies in the Bay Area, and one of the best is the Livermore Valley Opera. It is now presenting Donizetti’s great comedy opera The Elixir of Love. Opening night was last Saturday and there are two more performances this weekend. What makes the Elixir of Love so good is that it expresses the entire human condition perfectly. The Livermore Valley Opera orchestra got things off to a lively start with a neatly performed prelude conducted by music Director Alexander Katsman. Oh, how I wish that Donizetti had written a longer overture. To say that the entire production was first class is putting it mildly. It was absolutely top rate in every way. All of the singers had good voices and were fine actors. Nemorino, the male lead, was played brilliantly by tenor Christopher Bozeka. He sang the famous aria Una furtiva lagrima beautifully. I don’t think it is possible to do better. Elena Galvan played the female lead of Aldina. She has a beautiful, well modulated voice and all the power that you’d want. The other lead characters are also memorable. Andrew Potter played the arrogant military sergeant to perfection, and Samuel Weiser was the epitome of a snake-oil salesman. The story develops towards its inevitable conclusion. The magic elixir cures all the ills of the world. Hurray! It’s an easy drive to Livermore. Take in the show… You’ll love it.

The Walking on Wednesdays group tries to walk every safe walking Piedmont street during the year, and at the end of September there were only a few streets they hadn’t gotten to. Two of them were Kingston Avenue and the portion of upper Grand Avenue from Oakland Avenue to Pleasant Valley Road. On this section of Grand there is a new home being completed on a lot that was vacant for many years because it seemed unbuildable. Architects Jim Kellogg and Will Adams were on the walk and offered some observations. Kingston and the parallel Rose Avenue have some of the oldest homes in Piedmont. Quinoa, bulgur, wheat berries, couscous, or wild rice can be used in place of the brown rice. Butternut or acorn squash can replace the delicata, although I chose delicata because it cooks quickly, and the skin is edible. (You can skip the peeling, making it easy to prepare.) One small-medium squash. • 1/2 cup pomegranate arils • 1/2 cup celery, finely diced • 1/4 cup red onion, finely diced • 1/4 cup flat-leaf parsley, chopped INSTRUCTIONS Autumn Brown Rice Salad Makes about 2-quarts INGREDIENTS For the dressing: • 2 tablespoons sherry vinegar • 2 tablespoons olive oil, extra-virgin • 1/2 teaspoon Dijon mustard • 1/2 teaspoon sea salt, to taste • 1/4 teaspoon black pepper, freshly ground, to taste For the dressing: Combine the sherry vinegar, Dijon mustard, salt, and pepper in a small bowl. Whisk in olive oil until combined and emulsified. Set aside. Steam the brown rice according to package directions. Typically, one cup of raw rice will yield about two cups of cooked. The steamed rice should yield separate grains that are soft but retain a slightly chewy texture. Roast the delicata squash. Cut the squash lengthwise into quarters. Remove the seeds and membrane. Lightly brush with olive oil and roast at 350° F for about 30 minutes until tender and lightly browned. Cool slightly and dice to desired size. There is no need to peel the skin as it cooks up soft and tender. Combine the diced celery, red onion, and parsley in a 3-quart mixing bowl. articles.text: Editor: Elect Tom Ramsey and Re-elect Betsy Smegal Andersen and Jen Long to City Council On November 8, I’ll be proud to cast my vote for Tom Ramsey for City Council. I’ve had the great privilege of working with Tom for four years on Piedmont’s Planning Commission. I’ve been deeply impressed by Tom’s decision-making approach in evaluating renovation and construction projects. Tom emphasizes collaboration and cooperation between neighbors, and balances maintaining the character of the community with being open to design innovation. Tom’s many years of engagement and service in Piedmont reflect his dedication to our community. His professional experience and expertise as an architect and senior leader will be extraordinarily helpful to City Council as Piedmont moves forward with complying with state housing laws and completing major civic projects like the pool and civic center. Finally, Tom’s warm, collegial, and solutions-focused nature will ensure that different viewpoints are respected and reflected in the Council’s decisions on important issues facing our city. I look forward to electing Tom Ramsey to City Council. I also look forward to re-electing Betsy Smegal Andersenrn and Jen Long to City Council. As an experienced attorney, Betsy’s diligence and mastery of details will serve her well in her stewardship of our city. Betsy’s extraordinary dedication to Piedmont is reflected in her decades of service in the community. Betsy knows Piedmont inside and out and we are all better for it. I’ve had the privilege of knowing Jen Long since our children were in elementary school. Jen’s collaborative nature was invaluable in helping our school establish new health and wellness policies. Jen’s professional expertise as an attorney and her personal dedication to helping Piedmont become a more diverse and inclusive community have brought a welcome perspective to City Council. Piedmont will be in good hands with Tom, Betsy and Jen serving on City Council. I hope you’ll join me in casting your ballot for each of them in November. –Rani Batra Chair, Piedmont Planning Commission

articles.text: Editor: I am so inspired and excited about two of the school board candidates this year, Lindsay Thomasson and Ruchi Medhekar! I hope our community comes together to elect this Dream Team to the school board. Lindsay, Ruchi and I served on the Tri-School Site Council together where I saw firsthand their dedication to our schools, our children and to a collaborative process. During Site Council meetings, I was consistently impressed with the insightful questions and comments from each of them. It is clear that they both have taken the time and effort to dive deep into the inner workings of the district, and clear that their intent is always to meet the needs they see and hear from their fellow families. Each displays a level of tact and skill at working with groups, including administrators and teachers, and advocating hard for the families they were there to represent. I saw them patiently and diligently take time for extra meetings and one-on-ones with all the parties involved on issues until there was a clear path forward that worked for everyone. I have the bonus of being a Havens parent working alongside Lindsay and having experienced her incredible leadership when she was the Parent Club president from 2020-2021. We all know how difficult that year was, but Lindsay leaned into her role with kindness and repeatedly reminded the parent community to come together and have compassion for each other. The parent community felt ravaged after that school year, and instead of taking a much-deserved break from it all, Lindsay came back to help us repair and get our kids back on track emotionally and academically. At the same time, Ruchi was the parent club president at Beach School, and she and Lindsay have a history of working together.
